c.tagline: Where the Congo River meets vibrant Central African culture.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis run fixed routes with no meters; agree the fare (roughly 1,000-2,000 XAF in town) before getting in.

emergency.medical: 118 (fire/ambulance); response can be slow — hotels and embassies keep contacts for trusted private clinics

avoid.reason: Stay out of the outer southern districts (Makélékélé/Bacongo fringes) and unlit areas along the riverfront after dark, where street robberies occur.
Avoid photographing government buildings, the port, bridges or anyone in uniform — it can lead to detention — and watch valuables around Marché Total and other markets.

hood_desc: Brazzaville's downtown core along the Congo River, packed with government buildings, banks, and the city's international-standard hotels. Best for business travelers and anyone wanting easy access to embassies, restaurants, and riverside views.

A historic, densely packed quarter famous for its market and namesake school of painting, with lively, gritty street life. Suits budget travelers and culture seekers after an authentic local feel, though it's quieter on safety after dark.

A traditional residential district south of downtown known for its artisan markets and the colonial-era Case De Gaulle building. Good for travelers seeking cultural immersion and lower prices, a bit further from central attractions.

A leafy, mixed residential-commercial area centered on a well-known roundabout, popular with NGO staff and longer-stay visitors. Suits those wanting a quieter base with easy taxi access to the center.
The zone around Maya-Maya International Airport, home to several modern business hotels. Ideal for early flights or short layovers rather than sightseeing.

water.note: Tap water is not safe to drink; stick to bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (XAF) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no fare card or ticketing system for shared taxis or buses, so agree the price before boarding. Ferry tickets to Kinshasa are bought at the Beach Ngobila terminal.
transit.hours: Shared taxis and buses run roughly 6am-9pm; after dark, book a ride via Yango or arrange transport through your hotel rather than hailing on the street.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram, or urban rail; getting around relies on shared taxis, moto-taxis, a limited municipal bus service, and the Congo Ocean Railway for longer-distance travel to Pointe-Noire.

ferry: Beach Ngobila ferry to Kinshasa, DRC

tip.r: Not deeply embedded in local custom, but rounding up or leaving a small tip at restaurants and upscale hotels is appreciated, especially where a service charge isn't already included.

food.name: Saka-saka
food.desc: Pounded cassava leaves simmered for hours with palm oil, onion and smoked fish until dark and silky. The everyday green, eaten with rice or chikwangue.

places.name: Chez Gaspard
places.note: Known for traditional staples; the saka-saka and liboke are what regulars come for.

places.name: Poto-Poto ngandas
places.note: Neighbourhood open-air eateries doing classic Congolese plates for 1,000 to 4,000 FCFA.

places.name: Marche Total food stalls

food.name: Poulet moambe
food.desc: Chicken braised in thick palm-nut sauce with garlic and chilli, the dish both Congos claim as national. Served with rice, plantain or cassava loaf.

places.name: Pili Pili
places.note: Popular for moambe chicken and grilled capitaine, with live music some nights.

places.name: Mami Wata

places.name: Chez Gaspard
places.note: Home-style version at local prices in a relaxed nganda setting.

food.name: Makayabu
food.desc: Salted, dried cod rehydrated then fried or stewed with tomato, onion and pili-pili. Salty and intense, and best cut through with plain rice or plantain.

places.name: Marche Total food stalls
places.note: Sold dried by the slab and also cooked into plates at the market kitchens.

places.name: Poto-Poto ngandas

places.name: Marche Poto-Poto vendors
places.note: Rows of dried-fish traders; the smell tells you when you have arrived.

food.name: Liboke
food.desc: Fish or meat seasoned with chilli, onion and herbs, sealed in banana leaves and steamed over embers. The parcel is opened at the table, all steam and aroma.

places.name: Chez Gaspard
places.note: Reliable liboke of fish or meat cooked in banana leaves, alongside saka-saka.

places.name: Poto-Poto ngandas
places.note: Charcoal grills making mabokes to order in the evenings for very little money.

places.name: Mami Wata
places.note: Polished riverside take on the leaf-wrapped classic with a Congo River view.

food.name: Chikwangue
food.desc: Fermented cassava dough steamed in leaves into a dense, tangy loaf. Sliced and eaten with grilled meat or stews; sour, chewy and endlessly Congolese.

places.name: Marche Total food stalls
places.note: Bundles of leaf-wrapped loaves sold by the armful; buy one to eat with a grill plate.

places.name: Le Grilladin
places.note: Grill house for premium cuts of meat, served with cassava loaf and pili-pili.

places.name: Marche Poto-Poto vendors
places.note: Cheapest source, alongside cassava flour and fresh leaves.

food.name: Beignets
food.desc: Fist-sized fried dough balls, crisp outside and soft in the middle, sold hot from dawn by women working roadside pans. Breakfast for half the city.

places.name: Marche Poto-Poto vendors
places.note: Fried fresh from first light and handed over in paper; eat them warm.

places.name: Marche Total food stalls
places.note: Beignets with sweet coffee or ginger juice at the market entrances.

places.name: Marche Ouenze vendors

food.desc: Deep red hibiscus juice and fiery fresh ginger juice, both home-made, sweetened and served ice cold in bottles or frozen sachets. The default soft drink.

places.name: Mami Wata

food.name: Ngok and Primus lager
food.desc: Congolese beers brewed in Brazzaville and served in big cold bottles at every nganda. Ngandas also pour malafou, the tart fresh palm wine.

landmarks: Basilique Sainte-Anne du Congo
This striking green-tiled basilica with its soaring bell tower is Brazzaville's most photographed building, blending French colonial architecture with a distinctly African silhouette.
Mémorial Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza
This mausoleum honors the city's French founder and namesake, featuring marble halls and exhibits that trace Brazzaville's colonial and post-independence history.
Cathédrale de Brazzaville
Overlooking the Congo River, this historic cathedral with stained-glass windows and a graceful spire has served the capital's Catholic community since the early 20th century.
Palais du Peuple
This imposing presidential palace complex, built with Chinese assistance, stands as an architectural symbol of state power along the Congo River waterfront.
Zoo de Brazzaville
This city zoo gives visitors a chance to see native Congolese wildlife up close, including primates and birds, within a shaded green oasis in the capital.
Marché Total
One of Brazzaville's busiest markets, this bustling northside bazaar overflows with textiles, produce, and crafts, offering an immersive taste of local commerce and culture.
Corniche of Brazzaville
This riverside promenade along the Congo River offers postcard views across the water to Kinshasa, making it a favorite spot for evening strolls and photographs.
Stade Alphonse Massamba-Débat
Named after a former president, this national stadium is where Congolese fans gather for football matches and major public celebrations in the capital.
National Assembly Building
This government building, seat of the Republic of Congo's legislature, showcases a formal colonial-era facade that visitors pass on tours of central Brazzaville.
École de Peinture de Poto-Poto
This famed painting school, founded in 1951, launched a distinctive Congolese art movement celebrated for its bold colors and stylized figures, still active today.

train.note: No international trains. CFCO's domestic line runs from Brazzaville's Gare Centrale to the coast at Pointe-Noire (about 500 km, roughly 14-18h), historically the 'La Gazelle' passenger train every other day. Service has been repeatedly suspended (Pool-region conflict, poor track, flooding) and remains unreliable, so check locally that it is running; tickets are bought at the station and the CFCO website should be treated as informational only.

bus.note: No scheduled international coaches - the main crossing to Kinshasa is by river ferry, not bus. Long-distance domestic travel (Brazzaville-Pointe-Noire, Brazzaville-Ouesso) is handled by operators such as Océan du Nord, booked at their terminals; roads toward Cameroon in the far north are rough and used mainly by bush transport.

intl.op: Congo River public ferry & fast boats (canots rapides) from Beach Ngobila

ferry.note: The crossing to Kinshasa is one of the world's shortest international ferry hops (about 3-4 km, 15-30 min) but also one of the most bureaucratic: it leaves from Beach Ngobila and you must have a passport, DR Congo visa and exit paperwork sorted first. There is no online booking - buy at the terminal - and services can be interrupted by political tensions between the two capitals.
